overview: The Two Heaps pattern is an algorithmic design template that utilizes two separate heap data structures (typically a Max-Heap and a Min-Heap) to maintain balance and dynamically track partition boundaries within a set of elements. By storing the smaller half of the dataset in a Max-Heap and the larger half in a Min-Heap, this pattern allows for constant-time $O(1)$ access to median elements or boundary extrema, while supporting logarithmic $O(\log N)$ updates for insertions and deletions. It is primarily utilized in streaming data scenarios, scheduling algorithms, and optimization tasks where elements must be divided dynamically.
recognition_signals: Dynamic Streams: The input data arrives continuously as a stream, or is dynamically updated (insertions/deletions).
Partitioned Data Needs: The problem requires dividing elements into two distinct categories (e.g., smaller numbers vs. larger numbers, available capital vs. profitable projects).
Extrema/Median Queries: The task explicitly asks for the median of a stream, sliding window medians, or boundary values.
Logarithmic Constraints: The system expects insertions or updates to run in $O(\log N)$ time, and queries to run in $O(1)$ or near-constant time.

Greedy Multi-Phase Matching: Problems where you must evaluate candidates by one criterion (e.g., capital requirements) but select them based on a different criterion (e.g., maximum profit), requiring sorted order along two axes.

mental_model.analogy: Imagine a two-sided balanced balance scale holding weights in two baskets: a left basket and a right basket.
mental_model.description:
Imagine a **two-sided balanced balance scale** holding weights in two baskets: a left basket and a right basket.

To track the exact middle weight of all added items, you place the lighter half of the weights in the left basket (Max-Heap, so the heaviest of these light weights sits right at the top center) and the heavier half of the weights in the right basket (Min-Heap, so the lightest of these heavy weights sits at the top center). As you add new weights, you balance the baskets so that they have roughly the same number of weights. If the total number of weights is odd, one basket holds exactly one more weight. To find the median, you only need to look at the top weights of the two baskets, completely ignoring the unsorted clutter beneath.

brute_force_journey.brute_force_description: The brute force approach to tracking elements in a stream involves adding each incoming element to a list and sorting it completely before calculating the median.
brute_force_journey.inefficiency_observation: Overlapping subsegments perform duplicate evaluations of identical elements.
brute_force_journey.optimization_concept:
```
  Brute Force
  [Insert elements and sort the entire collection on every query -> O(N log N)]
       ↓
  Observation
  [To find the median, we only need the middle elements, not a fully sorted list]
       ↓
  Optimization
  [Split dataset into two balanced halves: Max-Heap (lows) and Min-Heap (highs)]
       ↓
  Final Pattern
  [Balanced Two Heaps: insert in O(log N) and query median in O(1)]
```

---

animation_steps.description: Insert element 3. Balance dictates pushing to Max-Heap (stores smaller half).
Insert element 5. Push to Min-Heap (stores larger half).
Calculate median: Average of Max-Heap top (3) and Min-Heap top (5) is 4.

variants.name: **Sliding Window Median**
variants.description: Max-Heap & Min-Heap (Same as stream median, with linear element eviction from the heaps.)

variants.name: **Maximize Capital**
variants.description: Min-Heap (Capital) & Max-Heap (Profits) (Move items from Min-Heap to Max-Heap based on capital constraints.)

variants.name: **Next Interval**
variants.description: Max-Start Heap & Max-End Heap (Match start-times to end-times by popping elements sequentially.)

common_mistakes.description: **Integer Division Precision:** When calculating the median of an even number of elements, dividing by `2` instead of `2.0` in languages like C++ or Java will truncate the decimal part, causing correctness errors.
**Heap Balance Check Timing:** Failing to balance the heaps after both insertions AND deletions. In sliding window variants, an element removal must always be followed by a rebalancing step.

**Inefficient Removals in Heaps:** Standard libraries (like C++ `std::priority_queue`) do not support $O(\log N)$ deletion of arbitrary elements. Implementing sliding window medians requires using custom heaps, trees (`std::multiset`), or lazy deletions to avoid $O(N)$ linear scans.
**Zombie elements in custom heaps:** Forgetting to clear pointers or map entries in custom heaps once item counters reach zero.

interview_perspective: Highly popular in FAANG/HFT rounds testing optimized traversals.

cheat_sheet: Keep the size difference between the two heaps at at most 1.

Always insert into the Max-Heap first if the list is empty, and then move elements to the Min-Heap if they exceed the size constraints. When performing lazy deletions in heaps, keep a secondary tracking table of deleted counts to avoid premature heap shrink actions.
